Most entrepreneurs try to build a business first and then cram their life around it.

I think that's a mistake.

Before you build anything, you should decide what your business is going to make possible in your life.

Here are some important questions to think through:

How many hours do you want to work?
How much income is actually enough?
Do you want weekends protected?
Do you want employees?
Do you want meetings?
Do you want to travel?

Those answers should help shape the business model that you eventually choose.

Because the answers affect what you sell, how you price it, how much complexity you install, and what kinds of customers you avoid.

You can build a "great" business and still build the wrong one for the life you want to live.

So define your life first.
Then build the business that supports it.

That was how I approached my one-person business, and it forced me to get excellent at a handful of skills:

Choosing the best work for me.
Keeping everything overly simple.
Protecting my time (especially weekends).
Creating predictable income with automation.
And growing without adding any complexity.

I learned so many lessons building my business this way. 

I took 7 of the most important ones and broke them down in a free 30-page guide on how I built my one-person business to $15M in profit.

It's hundreds of articles, hours of voice notes, and interviews with successful friends compressed into a short guide you can read in less than 30 minutes.

If you're great at what you do, but nobody knows, that's a "you" problem.

The market isn't going to discover you because you deserve it.

But, of course, someone half as talented is posting their work, explaining what they know, showing results, asking for the business, and getting paid.

Being uncomfortable with self-promotion is expensive.

But you don't need to become obnoxious.

You do need to get good at three things:

1. Show your work.

Talk about what you're building, what you're learning, what worked, and what failed. Be open, honest, and helpful.

2. Make your value extremely obvious.

Explain the problem you solve and show the result. Make it simple. A 6th-grader should be able to understand it.

3. Repeat yourself daily.

You are significantly more tired of your message than everyone else is. Most people missed it, forgot it, or are new to your world. Repeat!

People can't buy work they don't know exists.

And if you're building a one-person business, nobody else is coming to create that attention for you.

You have to learn how to get attention, earn trust, make good decisions, and turn your skills into income without spending your entire life doing it.

That took me years to figure out.

I wrote down everything I learned in a free solopreneur guide.

The 24/7 grinders won't experience the joy of a relaxed weekend with their spouse.

What a tragedy.

What's the point of doing all of this work if you never get the joy of downtime?

"Rise and grind."
"I'll sleep when I'm dead."

Lol. OK.

There's nothing wrong with hard work. I love working hard.

And there's nothing wrong with the occasional all-nighter or tough week, or workaholic month.

I get that. I've been there, too.

But if your identity is that work always gets 100% of your time, you're going to be a very sad and lonely person as you age.

If I could give one piece of advice to any aspiring entrepreneur, it would be this:

Build your life first and your business second.

Envision exactly how you want to live. What do your months, weeks, and days look like?

Then, fill in the gaps with exactly how work can support it.

I wrote down 30 pages of notes on how I did exactly that, and what skills were necessary (and unnecessary) to develop over time.

I hope you enjoy it. Cheers.

People waste months building things nobody wants because they get excited.

Just because the idea feels obvious to you doesn't mean the customer will care.

All they care about is whether your solution solves their problem at an appropriate price.

That's it.

That’s why building before validating is one of the worst habits.

You don't need six months of product building.

You need conversations.
You need a rough version.
You need someone to pay you.

A paying customer will teach you more than 100+ hours spent building something behind-the-scenes.

Quick, cheap, and dirty experimentation is one of the most valuable lessons I learned while building my one-person business to $15M.

Test cheaply. 
Learn quickly. 
Double down when the evidence is there.

This is one of the 7 skills that matter more than almost everything else when you're just getting started.

The new success stories won't be straight-line career paths.

They'll be "illegible careers."

Smart people, teaching themselves, and deploying tons of little experiments until something sticks.

There are so many ways to start:

Advise a business.
Build something useful.
Help someone solve a problem.
Design and launch an AI service.

Or do all of these and simply write about what you're learning.

Most experiments won't become businesses.

That's completely fine.

The whole point is to figure out what skills matter, what people care about and value, and which opportunities might be worth pursuing further.

Do that for a few years, and you'll never go linear on your career again.

The biggest benefit?

It becomes a lot harder for one company, one boss, or one bad quarter to wreck your income.

There are three important decisions that have an outsized impact on your life.

1. Who you marry

Who you marry isn't only about the best of times.

It's also about your support system in the most difficult times.

All in all, probably the most important decision you can make.

2. Where you live

The place you call home should align with your energy and the type of community you want to build.

Love that city chaos? Get in there.
Need that quiet country serenity? Find it.
Need both? Try your best to split your time.

3. How you earn a living

There's nothing worse than building a business that you hate working in.

A business can make you rich and still be a terrible business for you.

If it requires 80-hour weeks, some giant team you never wanted, or spending a ton of your time doing work you hate, money doesn't magically make that a good deal.

I always wanted something different.

A business that earned extremely well, stayed simple, and left me enough time and energy for the rest of my life.

Figuring out how to actually build that took me a decade.

The most successful people I know move fast.

Not chaotically. Fast.

There's a big difference.

Chaos means that you're doing fifty million things at once and not really getting anything done.

Fast (in this context) means eliminating everything that doesn't matter and committing only to the stuff that does.

When you operate this way, you naturally speed up.

You stop working on things that "feel" like they are moving your business forward, but are actually slowing you down:

- Designing a logo
- Reading more books
- Testing another software

And instead, you put something in front of potential customers, bad or not, and start getting critical feedback.

We're all in a race right now.

If you have an idea, unleash it to the crowd.

Let the market tell you where to spend your time.

This is one of several traits that successful solopreneurs and entrepreneurs develop quickly.

Comfort is overrated.

A lot of people want a life of coasting.

Easy work.
Easy money.
Easy decisions.
Easy schedules.

After a while, they just wake up feeling miserable.

Some of my best moments in life came from doing things that sucked.

Building skills I was terrible at.
Building a business nobody cared about.
Showing up when results were disappointing.
Making decisions I wasn't completely sure about.

The point isn't to remove pain from your life.

It's to choose difficulty that actually makes your life better.

True in life...true in business.

Do hard work, feel crappy for a bit, and reap the rewards of being out of your comfort zone.

It took me a decade to get even mildly decent at it.

Eventually, I put together a little field guide on the stuff I learned.

All condensed down to a guide you can read in 30 minutes.

A lot of people spend their 20s and 30s getting really good at one thing.

Work.

The income goes up.
The career gets better.
The calendar gets fuller.

Meanwhile, your relationship gets the leftovers.

Your health becomes something you'll "deal with later."

And eventually you realize you've built a pretty impressive life on paper that you don't particularly enjoy living.

But that's understandable.

It's hard to make progress without letting one part of your life eat the others.

Earn well.
Take care of your body.
Do work you actually enjoy.
Have time and energy for your family.

Nailing it all is hard.

It requires making some very different decisions about ambition, money, work, and what “enough” actually looks like in your life.

Tomorrow, I'm writing a short essay about it.

How the choices you make in your 20s, 30s, and 40s are very different. 

And what happens when you keep playing by the rules you made up when you were young.

It goes out tomorrow morning to 200,000+ readers.

Working for yourself means that nobody is coming to save you.

Every great decision you make, you get to bask in the glory.

Every terrible one, you get to own the repercussions.

Nobody is there to comfort you.
Or check in to see if you're OK.
Or hold your hand.

The buck simply stops with you.

For some people, that's absolutely terrifying.

It's what keeps them from ever getting started.

For other people, it's empowering.

Knowing that you own the entire ups and downs can feel liberating, powerful, and energizing.

Before you ever get into this game, it's important to understand what kind of person you are.

Because once all of that responsibility is yours, so are all of the decisions.

What to ignore.
Where to focus.
When to push harder.
When enough is enough.

I spent over a decade getting better at those decisions while building my one-person business to $15M.

Eventually, I narrowed the most important lessons down to 7 skills.

I break each one down in the free 30-page field manual at my LINK IN BIO.

Read it. Apply. Build a business you enjoy running.

If you want to make any money, somebody has to know you exist.

That’s the part a lot of really talented people struggle with.

They’re comfortable doing the work, but uncomfortable talking about it.

They don’t want to become the person constantly announcing how smart, successful, or busy they are.

I get that.

A lot of self-promotion can be excruciating to watch.

But there’s a big difference between talking about yourself and showing people what you know.

If nobody knows you exist, they can’t hire you.
If nobody sees your ideas, they can’t follow you.
If nobody knows your product, they can’t buy it.

That’s why learning to put yourself out there is such an important part of building a business.

You don’t need a million followers.
You don’t need to be an "influencer."
Or spend all day posting on social media.

You need a specific set of skills that help the perfect people find you, trust you, and pay you.

Figuring out what those skills are (and how they fit together) is the hard part.

I broke down the seven that helped me build a $15M one-person business in a free 30-page field manual called:

How I Built a $15M One-Person Business Without Destroying My Life.

A lot of business comes down to who you know.

And most people overcomplicate networking.

Trying to “add value.”
Asking for introductions.
Waiting for networking events.
Reaching out when they need something.

That's very 2015.

I’ve had much better luck doing something simpler:

When someone does work I genuinely admire, I tell them.

No ask.
No pitch.
No agenda.

Just a thoughtful little note explaining what I like about their work.

Do that consistently for a few years and watch what happens.

You start building real relationships with smart people.

Those people introduce you to other smart people.

Opportunities start showing up that you never could have planned for.

And your little business becomes much less dependent on cold networking and outreach.

This was one of the biggest lessons I learned building my little one-person business to $15M.

I was able to grow it because I got better at a handful of things that compounded over time.

Building trust.
Making good decisions.
Focusing on the right work.
Creating opportunities, not waiting.

And doing all of it without making the business my entire life.

This is one of 7 or 8 skills every entrepreneur needs to nail in order to be effective today.
